prompt:
Reference photograph of a single low STEPPED STONE BUTTRESS of about 1765, New England colonial masonry, the kind built against the wall of a brick meeting house, photographed as one detached object for 3D scanning. Only the buttress: no wall, no building, no ground plane beyond its own base course, no people, no text or watermark. Centred, the whole buttress inside the frame with clear margin all round, THREE-QUARTER VIEW from slightly below the top so the BROAD FLAT TOP SLAB and the stepped front and one side are all clearly visible at once. Plain light grey studio background, soft even daylight, no cast shadow.

PROPORTION IS CRITICAL AND IS THE POINT OF THE PLATE. This is a WIDE, LOW, BROAD-SHOULDERED block of masonry, not a tall thin pier and not a pinnacle:
- HEIGHT is about the same as the WIDTH (very slightly taller).
- DEPTH front-to-back is HALF the WIDTH.
So the silhouette is a squat rectangular mass, roughly as tall as it is wide and half as deep as it is wide. Do not draw a tall narrow pier; do not draw a gate post.

THE TOP IS A BROAD FLAT RECTANGULAR CAPPING SLAB AND IT IS THE WHOLE POINT.
- The buttress is finished with a single heavy dressed-granite COPING SLAB laid flat across the entire top, spanning the FULL WIDTH and the FULL DEPTH of the buttress and oversailing very slightly proud of the masonry beneath it on every side, with a plain chamfered drip edge under its lip.
- Its top face is FLAT, LEVEL, UNBROKEN and BROAD — a wide horizontal shelf a man could stand on with both feet, wide enough to lie across.
- ABSOLUTELY NO sloping weathering, NO gablet, NO pitched or pointed top, NO pinnacle, NO finial, NO tapering to a point, NO carving on the top. The top is flat.

THE STEPPING IS IN THE BODY BENEATH THE CAP, NOT IN THE CAP, AND IT IS EMPHATIC. The body is THREE CLEARLY SEPARATE STACKED STAGES of masonry, each one visibly smaller than the one below it, like a very short flight of three broad steps built of stone, so the profile of the front face is a staircase of three risers and two treads before the cap. The set-back at each step is a full hand's span, deep enough to throw a hard shadow line and to hold rainwater and moss. Do NOT draw a single plain unbroken block between plinth and cap.
Reading the total height from the base (0) to the top of the coping slab (1.0):
- 0.00 to 0.13  A projecting PLINTH COURSE, the widest and deepest course of the masonry, its top edge plainly chamfered, standing on a rough footing.
- 0.13 to 0.45  The lower stage of the buttress, set back a hand's breadth inside the plinth on the front and both ends.
- 0.45  A clear STEP: a narrow flat horizontal SET-OFF ledge running across the front and returning round both ends, where the masonry steps back again.
- 0.45 to 0.72  The middle stage, narrower and shallower than the lower one.
- 0.72  A second clear STEP, another narrow flat set-off, smaller than the first.
- 0.72 to 0.93  The upper stage, the narrowest of the three, still broad and square in plan.
- 0.93 to 1.00  The flat COPING SLAB described above, oversailing back out to the full width and depth of the plinth.
Each step must read as a real horizontal ledge with a visible top surface, catching the light along its edge. The stepping is on the FRONT face and the two END faces; the BACK face is a single plain flat vertical face from base to cap, because that face was built hard against the meeting house wall.

Details that must be present and readable: coursed rough-dressed grey New England granite in irregular courses, the blocks squared but not smooth, with wide lime-mortar joints struck flush and crumbling in places; the coping slab and the set-off ledges in better-dressed stone than the coursework; moss and dark green-black damp staining in the joints and in the angle of each set-off; pale lichen crust on the upper surfaces and along the cap's edge; old rain-streaking down the front; a chipped corner on the plinth.

Materials: weathered grey granite, cool grey-brown, damp at the foot; grey-white lime mortar; muted colours. Realistic period masonry, heavy and load-bearing, weathered and old, not stylised, not clean, not new. Photogrammetry reference plate style, evenly lit for 3D reconstruction, sharp and undistorted, full object visible.
